title: Engineered vs Solid Hardwood: Which Is Better for Kirkland's Damp Climate?
meta: Engineered hardwood handles Kirkland's humidity swings better than solid in most homes. Wills Flooring compares stability, refinishing, cost and room fit.
keywords: engineered vs solid hardwood, engineered hardwood vs solid hardwood humidity, best hardwood flooring for Pacific Northwest, engineered hardwood Kirkland WA, solid hardwood cupping wet climate
offers: Hardwood floor installation, engineered or solid

blocks.lead: For most Kirkland homes, engineered hardwood is the better choice: its cross-ply core moves far less than solid wood through our wet winters and dry summers, and Wills Flooring installs both at the same $3.25 per sq ft.
blocks.detail: Solid hardwood still wins in one case: a well-conditioned house over a wood subfloor where you want a floor that can be sanded five or six times over a century. The choice is about construction and location in the house, not quality. Both are real wood on top.

blocks.html: Kirkland is a hard place for wood floors to sit still. Houses in Juanita and Finn Hill sit over vented crawlspaces that run damp from November to April. Lakefront homes in Houghton live in air that never really dries out. Then July arrives, the heat pump runs, and indoor humidity drops thirty points in a month. That swing is the whole engineered-versus-solid debate. Here is how each floor handles it, honestly, and how we advise people who walk into our Lynnwood showroom from the Eastside.

blocks.text: What the two words actually mean

items.title: A real hardwood veneer over a plywood or HDF core
items.text: The top layer, called the wear layer, is genuine oak, hickory, maple or walnut, 2 to 6 mm thick. Under it, 5 to 11 plies run in alternating directions. The plies pull against each other, so the plank barely changes width when humidity changes. It can be nailed, glued or floated, and it can go on a concrete slab.

items.title: One piece of wood, top to bottom
items.text: Usually 3/4 in thick and 2 1/4 to 5 in wide, milled from a single board. Nothing restrains it, so it expands across its width in humid months and shrinks in dry ones. It is nailed to a wood subfloor, never floated or glued to concrete. It can be sanded down to roughly 3/32 in above the tongue, which is five or six refinishes.

blocks.text: Where each one belongs in a Kirkland home

a.title: Choose engineered when
items: The room is over a crawlspace that runs damp, or on a slab or daylight basement
You want planks 6 in or wider
The home has radiant heat or a heat pump that dries the air hard in summer
You are a tech buyer flipping in 7 to 10 years and want the modern wide-plank look for resale

b.title: Choose solid when
items: You are matching original 1970s to 90s oak in a Bridle Trails or Rose Hill home
The house has good crawlspace ventilation and stable humidity year-round
You plan to stay 20 or more years and want to refinish repeatedly
You prefer narrower strip flooring and a site-finished, gap-free look

items.html: Solid does not fail in Kirkland. Unmanaged solid does. Thousands of Kirkland homes have 30-year-old solid oak that looks great. Those homes have a dry crawlspace, a vapor retarder under the floor and heat that runs through winter.

The crawlspace decides more than the weather. We check crawlspace moisture and the subfloor reading at every estimate. A subfloor above 12 percent moisture is a problem for either floor, and a bigger one for solid.

Summer is the dangerous season for solid. People worry about the rain, but the winter swelling is gentle. It is the fast summer dry-down with the heat pump running that opens gaps and can split boards.

Lakefront is a special case. Houghton and Juanita Beach homes live at high ambient humidity year-round. That stable dampness is actually fine for either floor, as long as acclimation is done at that humidity, not in our warehouse.

Acclimation is not optional. Solid needs 5 to 7 days in the house at living conditions. Engineered needs 48 to 72 hours. Skipping this is the number one cause of the cupping complaints we get called to look at.

blocks.text: Three myths we hear on Eastside estimates

items.title: "Engineered is fake wood"
items.text: The surface you walk on is exactly the same oak or hickory as a solid board. A 4 mm wear layer is thicker than what most solid floors have left after two sandings.

items.title: "Solid adds more resale value"
items.text: Kirkland buyers and their inspectors look at species, width, finish and condition. Almost none can tell engineered from solid without pulling a register, and appraisers do not price them differently.

items.title: "Engineered can't be refinished"
items.text: Thin, builder-grade engineered cannot. A 3 mm or thicker wear layer sands the same way solid does. We do it regularly. Buy the wear layer, not the brand.

blocks.title: The trap to avoid:
blocks.text: The cheapest engineered floors have a 1 to 1.5 mm veneer. They look fine on day one and cannot survive a single sanding, so a deep scratch or a pet accident means replacement. For a Kirkland home you plan to keep, we recommend a 3 mm minimum and 4 mm if the budget allows. We show the cut edge of every sample at the estimate so you can see what you are buying.
How to decide in one visit

items.html: Start with the subfloor, not the showroom. Slab, crawlspace or basement rules out solid before you fall in love with a sample.
Pick a plank width. Anything over 5 in points to engineered in our climate.
Decide how long you are staying. Under 15 years, engineered at 3 mm is plenty. Over 20 and you love oak, solid earns its keep.
Compare wear layer, not price per box. Ask for the number in millimeters and get it on the quote.
Get labor and material on separate lines. Our labor is the same for both, published at the price list. If your project is over a slab, read hardwood over concrete first.

faq.q: Is engineered hardwood better than solid in a humid climate?
faq.a: For stability, yes. The cross-ply core resists the width changes that make solid wood cup in winter and gap in summer. Solid can still perform well in a humid climate if the crawlspace is dry, a vapor retarder is installed and the house holds 35 to 55 percent indoor humidity year-round.

faq.q: Does engineered hardwood cost less to install than solid?
faq.a: Not at Wills Flooring. Both are $3.25 per sq ft for installation labor. Unfinished solid is $2.75 plus sanding and finishing. Engineered often saves money on prep, because it can float or glue over a slab without building a plywood subfloor first, and it acclimates faster.

faq.q: How thick should the wear layer be on engineered hardwood?
faq.a: Three millimeters is the minimum we recommend for a home you plan to keep; it allows one careful refinish. Four to six millimeters allows two or three. Anything under two millimeters can only be screened and recoated, so a deep scratch means replacing the plank.

faq.q: Can solid hardwood be installed in a Kirkland daylight basement?
faq.a: Not directly on the concrete. Solid must be nailed to a wood subfloor, so you would build a plywood or sleeper system first, which adds cost and height and still leaves moisture risk. Engineered glued or floated over a tested, sealed slab is the standard answer.

faq.q: Does engineered hardwood affect resale value compared to solid?
faq.a: Not measurably in Kirkland. Buyers and appraisers respond to species, plank width, finish quality and condition. A 7 in white oak engineered floor typically shows better than a 2 1/4 in solid strip floor. Disclose what it is, and keep the spec sheet for the wear layer.

faq.q: How long does hardwood need to acclimate in Kirkland before installation?
faq.a: Solid needs five to seven days inside the house with the heat and normal living conditions running. Engineered needs 48 to 72 hours. We measure the subfloor and the boards with a moisture meter and install only when they are within about two percentage points of each other.
